title: Childhood
summary: Infancy (birth to 2 years), early childhood (2 to 6 years, the preschool stage), middle childhood (6 to 11 years) and adolescence (12 to 19 years). Infancy is the foundation of all development.

The sequence is fairly uniform across cultures but individual differences are large (one child walks at 10 months, another at 24). Milestones: lifting chin 1 month, rolling over 4 months, sitting alone 8 months, crawling 9 months, standing independently 9–10 months, walking alone about 15 months, running and climbing stairs 2 years, riding a tricycle 3 years, throwing a ball overhead 4 years, copying complex figures 6 years. Motor development supports the mother–child bond and mastery over the body. Gross motor development is control over large muscle groups (crawling, standing, walking). Fine motor development is control over small muscles of hands and fingers (grasping, pinching, holding a pencil).

Early childhood: locomotion becomes graceful; a 3-year-old runs straight and jumps; a 4-year-old skips, hops on one foot and catches a large ball; 5–6-year-olds ride a bicycle with training wheels and use the slide and swing. Fine motor: 2–3 years copies a circle and buttons large buttons; 3–5 years copies a square, prints own name and ties shoelaces; 5–7 years copies a triangle and prints numerals. Hand preference begins at 3–4 years; most children are toilet-trained by 4. Middle childhood: growth is gradual until the puberty growth spurt at 11–13; girls are slightly shorter than boys at 6–8 years but then taller and heavier; the spurt comes earlier in girls; children gain strength, speed, coordination and enjoy outdoor games.

Piaget's stages: sensori-motor (birth–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11) and formal operational (11+). Early childhood is the pre-operational stage with two sub-stages: symbolic function (2–4 years: mental images and symbols, pretend play, drawing; egocentrism – inability to see from another's point of view) and intuitive thought (4–7 years: asks 'why' and 'how come'; centration – focusing on one characteristic). Attention span grows (a 3-year-old 15–20 minutes, a 6-year-old an hour). Language explosion: about 900 words at 3 years and 8,000–14,000 by 6; grammar rules appear; bilingual children understand language better. Middle childhood (concrete operational): logical principles (conservation, transformation, seriation), better spatial reasoning, logical thinking limited to real and concrete situations, abstract concepts remain hard; language: synonyms, antonyms, prefixes and suffixes.

Early childhood: self-conscious emotions (shame, guilt), ability to modify emotional expression to the situation, empathy (depends on cognitive and language development), learning to control anger through guidance and role models. Play: parallel play (beside, not with), cooperative play (small group, pretend play), rough-and-tumble play (running, racing; learning to take turns and rules). Middle childhood: social comparison, seeing others' perspectives, pride and shame, mixed emotions, concealing emotions, internalised values and moral judgment; girls value interpersonal relations and family, boys social prestige; bullying (bullies often have demanding but unresponsive parents; victims are depressed with low self-esteem); self-concept shifts to personality traits and moves towards identity. Peer acceptance is important for self-esteem; a child liked by some and disliked by others is 'controversial'; temperament is an internal determiner of emotional development.

Socialization is the process of acquiring norms, values and beliefs significant in society and transmitting cultural values to children, including regulating and disciplining behaviour. Agents: parents and family, peers, school, religious institutions and mass media. In early childhood the family is primary; in middle childhood peers and school become prominent and stereotypes and prejudices develop. Parenting styles: authoritarian (demanding, controlling, insensitive), permissive (indulgent, non-demanding), authoritative (firm, consistent, gives reasons for discipline) and neglectful/uninvolved (uncaring, low control and communication). Ethnicity and socio-economic status also influence child development.

objective: Name the four sub-stages of childhood with ages.
Infancy (0–2), early childhood (2–6), middle childhood (6–11), adolescence (12–19).
Name any three gross motor skills.
Crawling, standing, walking, running, climbing (any three).
Name any three fine motor skills.
Grasping, pinching, holding a pencil, buttoning, cutting shapes (any three).
Name the four stages of Piaget's cognitive development.
Sensori-motor, pre-operational, concrete operational, formal operational.
(i) Inability to see the world from another person's point of view. (ii) Focusing on one characteristic of an object and basing judgment on it.
Fill in: (i) Development of empathy depends on ______ and ______ development. (ii) Playing without interaction is ______ play.
Fill in: (i) A child liked by some and disliked by others is called ______. (ii) An internal determiner of emotional development is ______.
Name any two agents of socialization.
Parents, family, peers, school, religious institutions, mass media (any two).
objective4: Name the two sub-stages of the pre-operational stage and their ages.
Symbolic function (2–4 years) and intuitive thought (4–7 years). Features: mental images and egocentrism; questioning and centration.
Identify the type of play: (i) children play beside each other without interaction; (ii) group pretend play; (iii) running, racing, climbing; (iv) learning to take turns.
(i) Parallel. (ii) Cooperative. (iii) Rough and tumble. (iv) Rough and tumble/cooperative play practising social rules.
Identify the parenting style: (i) demanding, controlling; (ii) indulgent, non-demanding; (iii) firm with reasons; (iv) uncaring, low control.
State the approximate age: (i) sitting alone; (ii) crawling; (iii) walking alone; (iv) riding a tricycle.
vsa: Differentiate gross motor from fine motor development.
Gross motor development is control of large muscles for crawling or walking; fine motor development is control of small muscles of hands and fingers for grasping or pinching.
Why is the study of physical and motor development important?
It is the basis for personality, social and emotional development, helps bonding with the mother figure and gives mastery over the body.
What is the 'language explosion' in early childhood?
Between 3 and 6 years the spoken vocabulary grows from about 900 words to 8,000–14,000 words and grammar develops.
Children (2–4 years) make and store mental images, pretend play with absent objects, talk about people and places and role-play, but show egocentrism.
Understanding and sharing another's feelings; an important component of positive social behaviour that depends on cognitive and language development.
The process of acquiring norms, values and beliefs considered significant in a society.
Victims of bullies are often depressed and have lower self-esteem.
sa: Describe physical development in middle childhood.

Growth is gradual until the puberty spurt at 11–13 years; girls are slightly shorter at 6–8 years but then taller and heavier, and their spurt comes earlier; children become stronger, faster and better coordinated and enjoy outdoor games.
Explain motor development in early childhood.

Locomotion becomes graceful: a 3-year-old runs and jumps, a 4-year-old skips and catches a ball, 5–6-year-olds ride a bicycle with training wheels; fine skills include copying shapes, tying laces and self-care such as brushing teeth; hand preference begins.
State the features of the pre-operational stage.
Use of symbols (words, images), pretend play and mental images, egocentrism, intuitive thought, centration and rapid language growth; thinking is not yet logical.
State the achievements of the concrete operational stage.
Understanding of logical principles (conservation, transformation, seriation), better spatial reasoning and advanced language, but logical thinking is limited to real and concrete situations.
Describe emotional development in early childhood.
Self-conscious emotions (shame, guilt) appear, children learn to modify emotions to suit situations, develop empathy and learn to control anger with guidance and role models.

Authoritarian is demanding and controlling; permissive is indulgent; authoritative is firm and consistent with reasons; neglectful is uninvolved and uncaring. Authoritative parenting suits socialisation best.
la: Describe physical and motor development in early and middle childhood.

Early childhood: graceful locomotion, running, hopping, skipping, catching; fine motor skills grow from copying circles to squares and triangles, ties laces, self-care; hand preference. Middle childhood: slower growth until the spurt, gender differences (girls' spurt earlier), better strength, speed and eye-hand coordination, games with rules. Milestones are uniform in sequence but individuals differ in timing.
Compare the pre-operational and concrete operational stages of Piaget.

Pre-operational (2–7): symbolic function, mental images, egocentrism, intuitive thought, centration, language explosion. Concrete operational (7–11): logical principles of conservation, transformation and seriation, improved spatial reasoning, logical thinking about real and concrete situations only, abstract concepts remain hard.

Early childhood: self-conscious emotions, emotion regulation, empathy, anger control, play from parallel to cooperative to rough-and-tumble. Middle childhood: social comparison, perspective taking, pride and shame, concealing emotions, moral judgment, gender differences, bullying, self-concept moving to traits and identity; peer acceptance supports self-esteem.
Explain socialization and the influence of culture, parenting style and other factors.

Socialization transmits norms, values and beliefs through parents, family, peers, school, religion and media; the family dominates early childhood and peers and school middle childhood, when stereotypes form. Parenting styles are authoritarian, permissive, authoritative and neglectful; ethnicity and socio-economic status affect family size, education, income and child development.
